brief.earned: You earn points by stating the center mu-1 minus mu-2 and the combined-variance spread formula correctly, and by justifying shape using both populations or both sample sizes, not just one of the two samples.
brief.loss: Checking the shape condition for only one of the two samples and treating that as sufficient for the whole difference's sampling distribution.
brief.move: State center as mu-1 minus mu-2, spread as sqrt(sigma-1-squared/n1 + sigma-2-squared/n2), then justify shape by checking both populations for normality or both n1 and n2 for the n >= 30 guideline -- a single sample meeting the condition is not enough.

core: x-bar-1 minus x-bar-2 is itself a random variable with a predictable center and spread built from both original samples, and its shape claim requires both samples to satisfy the normality condition, not just the larger or more convenient one.

criteria.fix: The mean of the sampling distribution of x̄1 − x̄2 is the difference of the population means, taken in the same order.
criteria.text: States that the mean of the sampling distribution is μ1 − μ2 = 502 − 500 = 2 g.

criteria.fix: Add σ1²/n1 and σ2²/n2 first, then take the square root; do not subtract or add standard deviations directly.
criteria.text: Calculates the standard deviation as √(6²/36 + 5²/30) ≈ 1.354 g.

criteria.fix: State the shape of the sampling distribution of the difference, not of the population distributions.
criteria.text: States that the sampling distribution of x̄1 − x̄2 is approximately normal.

criteria.fix: When population shapes are unknown, check that both sample sizes are at least 30 before claiming a normal shape.
criteria.text: Justifies the shape because both sample sizes (36 and 30) are at least 30, so the sampling distribution is approximately normal regardless of the population shapes.

criteria.fix: Replace n2 with 60 in the variance of the second sample mean, add the two variances, then take the square root.
criteria.text: Calculates the new standard deviation √(6²/36 + 5²/60) ≈ 1.190 g.

criteria.fix: Compare the new value with the earlier one and say which is smaller; a larger sample gives a smaller value.
criteria.text: States that the new standard deviation is smaller than the original 1.354 g.

prompt:
A calculator is permitted. Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) What is the mean of the sampling distribution of x̄1 − x̄2?

(b) Calculate the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of x̄1 − x̄2.

(c) Describe the shape of the sampling distribution of x̄1 − x̄2, and justify your answer.

(d) Suppose the inspector increases the sample from Machine 2 to 60 bags and keeps 36 bags from Machine 1. Calculate the new standard deviation of the sampling distribution of x̄1 − x̄2, and state whether it is smaller than, larger than, or the same as before.
stimulus:
Two machines fill bags of rice. Machine 1 fills bags with a mean weight of μ1 = 502 g and a standard deviation of σ1 = 6 g. Machine 2 fills bags with a mean weight of μ2 = 500 g and a standard deviation of σ2 = 5 g. The shapes of the two distributions of bag weights are not known.

An inspector takes an independent random sample of n1 = 36 bags from Machine 1 and an independent random sample of n2 = 30 bags from Machine 2, and computes the difference in the sample means, x̄1 − x̄2. Each machine fills at least 5,000 bags in a day.

core: The chi-square statistic sums (observed-expected)^2/expected across every cell of the table, and its expected-counts condition requires every expected count to exceed 5 -- a numerically different, lower threshold than the value-of-10 large-counts condition used for proportion and mean procedures elsewhere in this course; applying the 10-threshold here is a documented cross-topic confusion.

brief.earned: Points are earned when you interpret the p-value as the chance of a result at least as extreme, assuming the null hypothesis is true, show the required setup or condition check, and state the result in the language of the prompt.
brief.loss: Interpreting the p-value as the probability that the null hypothesis is true
brief.move: First name the quantity, structure, condition, or representation the prompt is really asking about; then interpret the p-value as the chance of a result at least as extreme, assuming the null hypothesis is true before doing arithmetic or writing the final sentence.

core: A p-value is the probability, computed assuming H0 is true, of getting a sample result at least as extreme as the one observed -- it is not the probability that H0 itself is true, since H0 is a fixed claim about the population, not a random event with its own probability; a small p-value means the observed result would be unusual if H0 were true, which is evidence against H0, not a probability attached to H0.

criteria.fix: Count simulated results as extreme as or more extreme than the observed value in the direction of Hₐ, including the observed value itself.
criteria.text: Estimates the p-value as 4/200 = 0.02 by counting the simulated samples with 20 or more riders who paid with the app (2 + 2 = 4).

criteria.fix: Name the event the p-value measures: a sample result at least as extreme as the observed one, in the direction of Hₐ, in context.
criteria.text: Describes the p-value as the probability of getting 20 or more riders who pay with the app in a random sample of 50 riders (a result as extreme as or more extreme than the one observed).

criteria.fix: End every p-value interpretation with the assumption, for example: assuming the true proportion of all riders who pay with the app is 0.25.
criteria.text: States that this probability is calculated assuming that the proportion of all the agency's riders who pay with the app is 0.25.

criteria.fix: Translate a small p-value into words: the observed result would rarely happen if H₀ were true, so it is evidence for Hₐ.
criteria.text: Explains that because the p-value (about 0.02) is small, getting 20 or more app users in a sample of 50 would be unusual if p were 0.25, so the data provide evidence that the proportion of all the agency's riders who pay with the app is greater than 0.25.

criteria.fix: Remember a large p-value means not enough evidence for Hₐ, never that H₀ is true; other values of p remain plausible.
criteria.text: Explains that a p-value that is not small means the observed result would not be unusual if p were 0.25, so it fails to provide convincing evidence for Hₐ, but it does not provide evidence that H₀ is true or prove that p = 0.25.

brief.earned: Points are earned when you choose homogeneity or independence from the study design, compute expected counts, and set df from the table dimensions, show the required setup or condition check, and state the result in the language of the prompt.
brief.loss: Using a goodness-of-fit test when the current Unit 3 scope only includes homogeneity and independence
brief.move: First name the quantity, structure, condition, or representation the prompt is really asking about; then choose homogeneity or independence from the study design, compute expected counts, and set df from the table dimensions before doing arithmetic or writing the final sentence.

core: Homogeneity (the same categorical variable measured across multiple populations or treatment groups) and independence (two categorical variables measured within one population) are a naming distinction only -- both use the identical chi-square statistic and identical expected-count formula, expected count = (row total)(column total)/table total; chi-square goodness-of-fit, which compares one sample to a fixed claimed distribution, was removed from the current AP Statistics course and is not tested.

criteria.fix: Use homogeneity when separate samples come from several populations and one categorical variable is compared; use independence for one sample and two variables.
criteria.text: Identifies a chi-square test for homogeneity, because the researcher took separate (independent) random samples from three populations (the adults of the three cities) and compares the distribution of one categorical variable, main news source, across those populations.

criteria.fix: Write homogeneity hypotheses about distributions of the categorical variable across populations, naming the variable and the populations, not about sample counts.
criteria.text: H₀: The distribution of main news source (television, online, other) is the same for adults in all three cities. Hₐ: The distribution of main news source is not the same for adults in all three cities (it differs for at least one city).

criteria.fix: Compare each sample size with 10% of the population it was drawn from, using the stated city population.
criteria.text: States that each sample of 150 is at most 10% of its city's adults: 150 ≤ 0.10(500,000) = 50,000.

criteria.fix: Check the expected counts, not the observed counts, and confirm every expected count is greater than 5 by naming the smallest one.
criteria.text: States that all expected counts are greater than 5 (the smallest is 19.3).

criteria.fix: Recall that chi-square distributions are skewed right and become less skewed as the degrees of freedom increase.
criteria.text: States that the chi-square distribution with 4 degrees of freedom is skewed right, and that the distribution with 10 degrees of freedom is less skewed (its skew is less pronounced).

criteria.fix: Link the statistic to its formula: each term compares an observed count with its expected count, so large values mean large departures.
criteria.text: Explains that the chi-square statistic measures the distance between observed and expected counts relative to the expected counts, so a large value indicates that the observed counts are far from the counts expected if the distributions were the same.

prompt:
A calculator is permitted. Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Identify the appropriate chi-square test, and explain why it is appropriate for this study.

(b) State the null and alternative hypotheses in context.

(d) If the null hypothesis is true, the test statistic has approximately a chi-square distribution with 4 degrees of freedom. Describe the shape of this distribution and how it compares with the shape of a chi-square distribution with 10 degrees of freedom. brief.earned: Points are earned when you use whether zero is inside the interval to support or reject a claim of difference, show the required setup or condition check, and state the result in the language of the prompt.
brief.loss: Concluding one group is larger when the interval includes zero
brief.move: First name the quantity, structure, condition, or representation the prompt is really asking about; then use whether zero is inside the interval to support or reject a claim of difference before doing arithmetic or writing the final sentence.

core: If the interval for p1-p2 excludes 0, that is convincing evidence of a real difference between the two population proportions; if the interval contains 0, that is insufficient evidence of a difference -- because 0 (meaning p1=p2, no difference) remains a plausible value for p1-p2, even when most of the interval sits on one side of 0.

criteria.fix: Name the parameter fully: the difference in the proportions of all adults in each town who used a library, and say which town is subtracted.
criteria.text: States that we are 95% confident that the interval from 0.046 to 0.174 captures the difference (Riverton minus Lakeside) between the proportions of all adult residents of each town who used a public library in the past month.

criteria.fix: Describe the long-run capture rate: in repeated random samples of the same sizes, about 95% of intervals would contain the true difference.
criteria.text: Explains that if many pairs of independent random samples of 500 Riverton adults and 400 Lakeside adults were taken and a 95% interval calculated from each pair, about 95% of the intervals would capture the true difference p₁ − p₂ in the proportions of adults who used a public library in the past month.

criteria.fix: To judge a claimed difference, check whether 0 is in the interval; if 0 is excluded, there is convincing evidence of a difference.
criteria.text: States that the interval supports the first claim (gives convincing evidence of a difference) because 0 is not in the interval; every plausible value of p₁ − p₂ is positive.

criteria.fix: Convert percentage points to a difference, here 0.20, and check whether any plausible value in the interval is as large as that.
criteria.text: States that the interval does not support the second claim because every plausible value of p₁ − p₂ is less than 0.20 (0.20 is above the upper limit 0.174).

criteria.fix: Remember that confidence is not certainty: a sample-based interval may or may not contain the parameter, so never say it must be inside.
criteria.text: Explains that the interval is calculated from random samples, so it may or may not contain the true difference; the 95% confidence level means about 5% of such intervals miss the true difference.

prompt:
A calculator is permitted. Answer all parts of the following question.

(a) Interpret the 95% confidence interval in context.

(b) Interpret the 95% confidence level in context.

(c) One board member claims that the proportions of adults who used a public library in the past month are different in the two towns. A second board member claims that Riverton's proportion is more than 20 percentage points higher than Lakeside's. Does the interval support each claim? Explain.

(d) A resident says, "Since the interval was calculated from the data, the true difference p₁ − p₂ must be between 0.046 and 0.174." Explain why the resident's statement is not correct.
stimulus: A regional library board selected a random sample of 500 adult residents of Riverton and, independently, a random sample of 400 adult residents of Lakeside. Each town has more than 20,000 adult residents. In the samples, 230 of the Riverton residents (0.46) and 140 of the Lakeside residents (0.35) said they had used a public library in the past month. All conditions for inference were met, and the board calculated a 95% confidence interval for p₁ − p₂, where p₁ is the proportion of all adult residents of Riverton who used a public library in the past month and p₂ is the proportion of all adult residents of Lakeside who used a public library in the past month. The interval is (0.046, 0.174).

brief.earned: You earn points by connecting molecule breakdown, electron carriers, proton gradients, oxygen, and ATP production.
brief.loss: Saying oxygen makes ATP directly instead of explaining its role as final electron acceptor.
brief.move: Track carbon, electrons, and ATP through the process instead of memorizing a list of stages.

core: Cellular respiration transfers energy from organic molecules to ATP through glycolysis, oxidation steps, and electron transport, and this same core process -- along with fermentation, which lets glycolysis continue without oxygen by producing alcohol or lactic acid -- occurs in some form across all living organisms, not only in organisms with mitochondria.

criteria.fix: Glycolysis: 6C glucose → 2× 3C pyruvate (no CO₂). Pyruvate oxidation: 2 pyruvate → 2 CO₂ + 2 acetyl-CoA (2C). Krebs ×2: 2 acetyl-CoA → 4 CO₂. Total: 6 CO₂ = all 6 glucose carbons accounted for.
criteria.text: Describe glucose breakdown through the three stages in general terms and identify CO2-releasing steps.

criteria.fix: Glycolysis: 2 NADH (cytoplasm). Pyruvate oxidation: 2 NADH (matrix). Krebs ×2: 6 NADH + 2 FADH₂ (matrix). Total: 10 NADH + 2 FADH₂. Mitochondrial NADH → Complex I (4H⁺/NADH). FADH₂ → Complex II (no H⁺ pumped). Cytoplasmic NADH: shuttle dependent (2.5 or 1.5 ATP equiv).
criteria.text: Identify which stages produce NADH/FADH2 and explain their general role feeding the ETC.

criteria.fix: Three reasons: (1) proton leak across inner membrane dissipates gradient as heat; (2) ATP-ADP translocase uses part of proton gradient to export ATP; (3) cytoplasmic NADH must use less efficient shuttles (glycerol-3-phosphate gives fewer ATP); (4) non-integer P/O ratio for ATP synthase.
criteria.text: Explain at least two general reasons actual ATP yield is lower than theoretical maximum.

criteria.fix: Pasteur effect: anaerobic = 8× more glucose consumed. Aerobic: ETC produces ~30 ATP/glucose; high ATP inhibits PFK-1 → glycolysis slows. Anaerobic: no ETC → only 2 ATP/glucose; low ATP → PFK-1 uninhibited → glycolysis runs fast; fermentation regenerates NAD⁺ to keep glycolysis going. Net: must consume much more glucose to maintain ATP.
criteria.text: Explain increased anaerobic glucose consumption via ATP needs, fermentation's lower yield, and NAD+ regeneration.

prompt:
Answer all parts of the following question.

Part A: Describe, in general terms, how a glucose molecule (C₆H₁₂O₆) is broken down through glycolysis, pyruvate oxidation, and the Krebs cycle, and identify at which of these stages CO₂ is released.

Part B: For one molecule of glucose completely oxidized through aerobic respiration, explain which stages produce NADH and FADH₂, and explain how these electron carriers are used in the electron transport chain to ultimately produce ATP.

Part C: The actual ATP yield from one glucose molecule is lower than the theoretical maximum. Explain why, describing at least TWO general reasons the process is not perfectly efficient.

Part D: A cell is shifted from aerobic to anaerobic conditions. Using the data in Table 1, which shows glucose consumption rates, explain why glucose consumption increases dramatically under anaerobic conditions. Your answer should connect the cell's ATP needs, the lower ATP yield of fermentation compared to aerobic respiration, and the need to regenerate NAD⁺ for glycolysis to continue.
stimulus:
Table 1: Glucose consumption in yeast cells
Condition     | Glucose consumed (mmol/hr/g cells)
Aerobic       |        0.5
Anaerobic     |        4.2

General ATP yield summary:
Glycolysis: net 2 ATP (substrate-level), 2 NADH
Pyruvate oxidation: 0 ATP, 2 NADH
Krebs cycle (×2 turns): 2 ATP (GTP), 6 NADH, 2 FADH₂
Each NADH and FADH₂ used in the electron transport chain contributes to ATP production, but not with perfect efficiency.

brief.earned: You earn points by connecting molecule breakdown, electron carriers, proton gradients, oxygen, and ATP production.
brief.loss: Saying oxygen makes ATP directly instead of explaining its role as final electron acceptor.
brief.move: Track carbon, electrons, and ATP through the process instead of memorizing a list of stages.

core: Cellular respiration transfers energy from organic molecules to ATP through glycolysis, oxidation steps, and electron transport, and this same core process -- along with fermentation, which lets glycolysis continue without oxygen by producing alcohol or lactic acid -- occurs in some form across all living organisms, not only in organisms with mitochondria.

criteria.fix: Four evidence: (1) size/shape similar to bacteria; (2) double membrane (inner = bacterial membrane with cardiolipin); (3) circular naked mitochondrial DNA; (4) 70S ribosomes (sensitive to bacterial antibiotics). Gene transfer: most mitochondrial genes transferred to nucleus over evolution (endosymbiotic gene transfer) for better regulation, protection, and coordination.
criteria.text: Describe two or three lines of evidence for endosymbiosis (double membrane, own circular DNA, 70S ribosomes, binary fission).

criteria.fix: H⁺ pumped from matrix to intermembrane space by Complexes I (4H⁺), III (4H⁺), IV (2H⁺) as electrons flow. Proton gradient (proton-motive force) drives H⁺ back through ATP synthase F₀ channel → F₁ rotation → ATP synthesis from ADP + Pi. Complex IV reduces O₂ to H₂O (final electron acceptor).
criteria.text: Explain (i) proton gradient source, (ii) how it drives ATP synthase, (iii) the general role of ETC complexes in building the gradient -- score (i)/(ii)/(iii) separately.

criteria.fix: Rotenone: O₂ decreases (ETC blocked at Complex I), ATP decreases. Oligomycin: O₂ decreases (back-pressure stops ETC), ATP decreases. DNP: O₂ increases (no back-pressure, ETC runs faster), ATP decreases (gradient dissipated as heat).
criteria.text: Predict rotenone (decreases both), oligomycin (ATP synthesis decreases; O2 consumption also decreases per the stimulus note on coupled electron flow, or unaffected with sound reasoning accepted), and DNP (O2 consumption increases, ATP synthesis decreases) with reasoning for each.

criteria.fix: Heart/neurons have high continuous ATP demand → many mitochondria; cristae (inner membrane folds) increase surface area for ETC/ATP synthase. Fission inhibition: neurons need small mitochondria transported to distant synapses via microtubules; without fission, elongated mitochondria cannot enter axons/dendrites → synapses lack ATP → neurotoxicity. Fibroblasts are small and divide frequently — less dependent on mitochondrial transport.
criteria.text: Explain why heart cells need many mitochondria and describe cristae as the structural feature that maximizes ATP output.

prompt:
Answer all parts of the following question.

Part A: The endosymbiotic theory proposes that mitochondria evolved from free-living bacteria engulfed by an ancestral eukaryotic cell.
Describe TWO OR THREE specific lines of evidence that support the endosymbiotic origin of mitochondria.

Part B: Describe the role of the inner mitochondrial membrane in ATP synthesis. In your answer, explain: (i) the source of the proton gradient; (ii) how the proton gradient drives ATP synthesis through ATP synthase; and (iii) the general role of the electron transport chain complexes (supplied in the stimulus) in building that gradient.

Part C: A researcher adds the following compounds to isolated mitochondria respiring aerobically. For each compound, predict whether O₂ consumption and ATP synthesis will increase, decrease, or be unaffected, and explain your reasoning:
Rotenone (inhibits Complex I electron transfer)
Oligomycin (blocks the F₀ channel of ATP synthase)
Dinitrophenol / DNP (uncoupler — makes the inner membrane permeable to H⁺)

Part D: Heart muscle cells have unusually high numbers of mitochondria. Explain the functional reason for this, and describe the specific structural feature of mitochondria that maximizes ATP output.
stimulus:
Mitochondrial structure:
• Outer membrane: permeable to small molecules (porins)
• Intermembrane space: H⁺ accumulates here during electron transport
• Inner membrane: highly folded into cristae; contains electron transport chain (ETC) complexes and ATP synthase; impermeable to ions
• Matrix: contains Krebs cycle enzymes, mtDNA, mitochondrial ribosomes

The electron transport chain complexes in the inner membrane pump H⁺ into the intermembrane space as electrons pass through them; ATP synthase uses the resulting H⁺ gradient to synthesize ATP. Note: when the H⁺ gradient cannot be relieved by ATP synthase (e.g. if ATP synthase is blocked), electron flow through the chain and O₂ consumption also slow, because the chain works against the built-up gradient.
